By and By
bye-and-BYE
adverb
From the preposition by doubled and used adverbially in older English to mean “in close order, one hard upon another,” and so “straightway, at once”; the modern sense of “after a while, eventually” is a later softening of the very same phrase.

Biblical Definition

By and by in the KJV does not mean “eventually,” as our ears now take it. It means immediately, at once, this very moment. The word is turned clean around: what once named the shortest interval now names a long one. Scripture will not let the mistake stand. When Herod’s dancing girl was prompted by her mother, she came in with haste and demanded, “I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist” (Mar 6:25) — not someday, but now, before the feast cooled and the king’s rash oath could cool with it. So too in the parable of the sower: the stony-ground hearer receives the word with joy, yet hath no root in himself, and when tribulation ariseth, “by and by he is offended” (Mat 13:21) — his fall is not slow apostasy but instant collapse the moment the sun is up. And the Lord teaches the servant’s place with it: which of you will say to a servant come from the field, by and by, “Go and sit down to meat” (Luk 17:7)? The immediacy is the whole point. Yet the same phrase can sound a sober warning: of wars and commotions the Lord says “the end is not by and by” (Luk 21:9) — not immediately, whatever the alarmists cry. The reader who softens by and by into “presently, in time” loses the very urgency the Holy Ghost pressed into it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Immediately; at once; straightway — not, as now, “after a while.”

expand to see more

BY AND BY, immediately; at once; without delay.

From by repeated, in the old sense of “in close order, one hard upon another.”

The modern “after a while, presently” is a later weakening of the phrase.

The dancer asked the Baptist’s head “by and by” — that instant (Mar 6:25).

The stony hearer is offended “by and by” — the moment trouble comes (Mat 13:21).

Key Scripture

Mar 6:25 — "And she came in straightway with haste unto the king, and asked, saying, I will that thou give me by and by in a charger the head of John the Baptist."

Mat 13:21 — "Yet hath he not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended."

Luk 17:7 — "But which of you, having a servant plowing or feeding cattle, will say unto him by and by, when he is come from the field, Go and sit down to meat?"

Luk 21:9 — "But when ye shall hear of wars and commotions, be not terrified: for these things must first come to pass; but the end is not by and by."

Modern Corruption

A word turned inside out: the AV’s “by and by” means now, while ours means later — and the urgency is lost with the change.

expand to see more

Here is a genuine reversal of sense, and it must be named, for it misleads every modern reader of the Gospels. In the Authorized Version “by and by” means immediately; in our speech it means eventually, after a while, when we get round to it. The two are opposites. A reader who does not know it will picture the stony-ground hearer drifting slowly from the faith, when the Lord says he is offended by and by — the instant the heat rises. He will imagine Herod’s court taking its leisure over John, when the girl demanded the head that moment. The drift is not wicked, only worn: a phrase for the sharpest haste has been rubbed down into a phrase for delay.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the immediacy of God’s summons and man’s response. Scripture is full of now: today if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts; behold, now is the accepted time. The stony hearer’s ruin was instant because his root was never there, and the sun that should have ripened him withered him instead. Against him stands the servant who obeys at once, and the Master who bids His own watch, for they know not the hour. The softening of “by and by” into “someday” is the very disease of the natural heart, which hears the call of God and answers, later. The word as the KJV meant it rebukes the delay: not by and by, but now.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means immediately, at once — the sharpest haste, not the leisured “eventually” of modern speech.

expand to see more

By and by — the preposition by doubled and used adverbially.

In older English it meant “in close succession,” hence “straightway, at once.”

The modern sense “after a while” is a weakening of the same phrase.

The dancer demanded the Baptist’s head by and by — that instant (Mar 6:25).

The stony hearer is offended by and by, the moment trouble comes (Mat 13:21).

Usage

"By and by means now, not later: the girl wanted John’s head that very moment."

"“By and by he is offended” — the stony hearer falls at once, not by slow degrees."

"“The end is not by and by”: not immediately, whatever the setters of dates may cry."
